To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) unsupervised morpheme labelling is possible, (ii) EMMA is a useful and robust metric to compare algorithms, (iii) PROMODES is a powerful probabilistic generative word decomposition model, (iv) the decision threshold is an important parameter that can be optimised, (v) combining different models can improve the overall performance, (vi) DEAP is the first deductive abductive parser for morphologically complex languages that is capable of learning the grammar from

unsupervised learning is possible and that it can be combined with a supervised approach to achieve better results than either approach alone, that the EMMA metric is a good choice for evaluating the quality of word decomposition and that the DEAP approach is a promising method for labelling morpheme boundaries in an unsuperved manner.

(1) the unsupervised morpheme labelling algorithm DEAP outperforms other algorithms in the task of morphological analysis of Zulu, (2) unsupervised morphometric analysis can be used as a first step towards morphological POS tagging and (3) the unsupervized algorithm PROMODES is a good starting point to build a word decomposition system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of machine learning techniques in the context of the automatic analysis of morphologically rich languages.
the development and the application of machine learning algorithms for the analysis of under resourced languages.
the analysis of morphological complexity in agglutinating and inflecting languages and demonstrates that unsupervised machine learning can successfully be applied to the task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
machine learning is a viable approach for the analysis of agglutinating morphologically complex languages and that it can be used to improve existing methods.
the presented algorithms can be applied to morphologically complex languages, but the results are still not competitive to those of linguistically motivated rule based systems.
machine learning has been shown to be applicable to the morphological analysis of agglutinating and fusional languages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results are promising, but that more work needs to be done to improve them.
the proposed approaches are able to achieve state of the art results in the field of morphological analysis and that they are applicable to languages of different typologies and complexity.
the algorithms are able to learn the morphotactics of the languages and that they perform better than the baseline.
The main takeaway from our work is that
machine learning is a promising approach for the analysis of agglutinating morphologically complex languages and can be applied in many different ways to automate this task.
unsupervised learning can be used to analyse agglutinating morphological structures, and that the performance of the algorithms is comparable to that of supervised methods.
machine learning can indeed be applied to the analysis of morphological complexity and can provide valuable insights for linguistic analysis.
